analysis.one_liner: Caps prescription drug copays at $200 per drug and $500 per month for people with Medicare or private insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its October 2009 introduction it sat in three House committees until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have limited how much people with Medicare drug coverage or private health insurance can be charged out of pocket for prescriptions. No single prescription could require a copay or coinsurance above $200 a month, and total drug copays could not exceed $500 a month, with the caps rising with inflation. It would also have made it easier for Medicare beneficiaries to get plan approval for expensive specialty drugs, and ordered a study of eliminating drug cost-sharing for beneficiaries whose out-of-pocket costs top 5% of income.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries with high drug costs and people with private insurance who need expensive specialty drugs. Under the bill, no one with drug coverage could be charged more than $200 a month for one prescription or $500 a month for all their prescriptions combined, and Medicare enrollees could ask for an exception to be charged the lower non-preferred rate for a specialty drug.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries and insured patients on costly drugs

how_it_helps.text: Caps Medicare Part D and private-insurance drug copays and coinsurance at $200 per drug per month and $500 total per month, adjusted annually for inflation [S2][S3].
Prevents plans from charging a patient more than the base cost of the drug itself, a limit aimed at plans that charge more in copays than the drug is worth [S3].
Expands the Medicare formulary exception process so beneficiaries can request that a specialty drug be treated as a non-preferred drug, which typically carries a lower copay [S2][S3].
Directs MedPAC to study eliminating drug cost-sharing for Medicare beneficiaries whose out-of-pocket drug costs exceed 5% of income, laying groundwork for further relief [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, Medicare Part D plan sponsors, and employers offering group health coverage would bear the cost of covering drug charges above the caps, which could flow into higher premiums or plan costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: Capping what patients pay does not cap what drugs cost, so plans and employers would absorb the difference, likely through higher premiums shared by all enrollees [S3].
The caps rise automatically with inflation, so the protection would erode over time as drug prices grow faster than general inflation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing catastrophic drug bills, the caps would be substantial and immediate protection; a $500 monthly ceiling on total drug copays directly addresses the specialty-drug cost-sharing practices the bill also ordered studied. The honest cost is that the money has to come from somewhere: premiums and plan sponsor payments would rise, and without acting on underlying drug prices the relief is a cost shift rather than a price fix. The bill's own proposed studies suggest its sponsors saw it as a first step rather than a complete answer.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the bill on October 13, 2009, with eight original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to three committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — meaning each could consider only the parts touching its jurisdiction [S1][S3].
Within days it was sent to subcommittees on health, the level where bills typically die [S5].
Twenty-four Democrats cosponsored the bill; no further action of any kind was recorded for the rest of the 111th Congress [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and Medicare Part D plan sponsors are better off, since the caps on drug copays and specialty-tier practices they would have faced never became law. Patients with high drug costs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and Part D plan sponsors

for.name: Rep. Henry C. 'Hank' Johnson Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill capping prescription drug copays under Medicare and private insurance

against.name: House committees of jurisdiction
against.role: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor committees and their health subcommittees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 24 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never advanced beyond committee referral in the Democratic-controlled House.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: The bill would cap the copays and coinsurance these plans can charge for any drug at $200 a month, or $500 total, and limit specialty-tier cost-sharing. Plan sponsors would have to absorb drug charges above those caps. The bill died in committee, so these limits never took effect.
Employers who sponsor group plans would have shared the cost of the caps alongside insurers. Their enrolled employees would have gained the same out-of-pocket protection.

Caps on what patients pay per prescription make expensive drugs easier for patients to afford, which can raise prescription uptake. The bill does nothing to lower manufacturers' prices, so their revenue is largely untouched.
